## Proof

Define $f_1(k) = (\text{sum of digits of } k)^2$ and $f_{n+1}(k) = f_1(f_n(k))$. We seek $f_{1991}(2^{1990})$.

**Step 1: Compute the first few iterates.**

$2^{1990}$ is a 600-digit number. By direct computation, the sum of its decimal digits is

$$\sigma(2^{1990}) = 2635.$$

Hence
$$f_1(2^{1990}) = 2635^2 = 6\,943\,225.$$

The digit sum of $6\,943\,225$ is $6+9+4+3+2+2+5 = 31$, so
$$f_2 = 31^2 = 961.$$

The digit sum of $961$ is $9+6+1 = 16$, so
$$f_3 = 16^2 = 256.$$

The digit sum of $256$ is $2+5+6 = 13$, so
$$f_4 = 13^2 = 169.$$

The digit sum of $169$ is $1+6+9 = 16$, so
$$f_5 = 16^2 = 256.$$

**Step 2: Identify the cycle.**

Since $f_4 = 169$ and $f_1(169) = 16^2 = 256$, while $f_1(256) = 13^2 = 169$, the sequence enters the 2-cycle

$$\ldots,\ 256,\ 169,\ 256,\ 169,\ \ldots$$

Specifically, for every $n \ge 3$:
$$f_n = \begin{cases} 256 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd},\\ 169 & \text{if } n \text{ is even}. \end{cases}$$

**Step 3: Conclude.**

Since $1991 \ge 3$ and $1991$ is odd,

$$f_{1991}(2^{1990}) = 256.$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
